description: I’m Sai Vignesh, a 5th-grade student who loves space, Mars and building games. I chose the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge because I’m a junior myself, and I wanted to show that kids my age can train like astronauts using real NASA data. So I built MARSMISSION, where players repair a Mars base, restore power and rescue a rover while learning how real missions work.
summary:
MARSMISSION is an educational Mars outpost survival game built with Python and Pygame CE. Players complete three campaign missions: restoring a communication blackout by repairing and aligning an antenna, rebuilding a failed power circuit and allocating energy in the shelter, and rescuing a stranded rover by scanning, repairing, route-planning and driving across Martian terrain.
An optional Research Terminal turns real NASA data into learning activities. Players explore HiRISE and MOLA terrain imagery, Perseverance rover camera views, THEMIS thermal context, solar-panel dust imagery, and MEDA dust-opacity timelines from published Jezero crater studies, then apply what they learn to in-game decisions, such as picking a calmer dust window for rover travel. Research earns points for a supply store.
The game makes space science engaging and accessible by letting players think like mission engineers, applying real concepts of communications, power, dust, terrain and navigation. It runs offline as a packaged Windows/macOS app with auto-save and mission replay. All data is credited to NASA, JPL, the University of Arizona and USGS, with no fabricated measurements.
details:
MARSMISSION

Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer · NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

The problem we set out to solve

Mars science is usually met through articles, images and datasets that students read but never use. The ideas that make a Mars outpost work, such as pointing a dish at the right satellite, sharing limited power between life support and equipment, and planning a drive through a dust storm, stay abstract until someone has to make the decision under pressure. Real NASA data is also hard to approach: file formats, instrument names and units put off beginners before they reach the science.

Our answer is a game in which a dust storm has damaged a research base and the player must bring it back to life. Every mission is a small engineering problem, and the optional research activities show where the real-world version of that problem comes from.

What we built

MARSMISSION is a 2.5D Mars outpost game for Windows, built with Python and Pygame CE. The player is a young astronaut at a research base on Mars that a dust storm has damaged. Nothing works until the player repairs it. The player walks through the base and the terrain around it, collects repair materials, and goes to mission stations to restore the base's systems one at a time.

The game has four parts that work together:

  • The base world. An explorable area with the habitat, the Research Lab, the supply store and the mission stations, drawn with layered parallax scenery. An inventory (I) and a journal (J) help the player track what they have and what to do next.
  • The three-mission campaign. Communication Blackout, Shelter Power Emergency and Rover Rescue, played in order. Each mission has a prep screen, a timer, clear on-screen feedback and a debrief with a mission report.
  • The Research Terminal. An optional station where the player studies real NASA imagery and data and completes short activities.
  • The supply store. Research Points earned in the terminal are spent on kits and supplies that help with repairs, which connects learning to progress without blocking anyone.

The whole game ships as one download. A player unzips it and double-clicks MARSMISSION.exe. It needs no internet connection, no account and no Python installation.

The core idea

The game is built on four ideas:

  • Learn by fixing something that matters. Each mission restores a system the colony needs: communications, power, then a rescue. The player sees the result of each decision on screen.
  • Real data supports the decisions. Research activities use curated NASA products so that choices such as when to travel or how to think about dust have a scientific reason.
  • Research helps but never blocks. Research is optional. It earns Research Points for the supply store, but it is not needed to unlock the next mission, so every player can finish the campaign.
  • Honest about what is real. Real NASA material is labelled and credited. Game values, such as habitat power units, are marked as fictional.

The campaign

The player explores the base and the surrounding terrain, collects repair materials, and uses stations such as the Research Lab, the supply store and the rover garage. Three missions are played in order, and each one unlocks the next. Progress saves automatically, and a final report closes the campaign. A new campaign can be started after confirmation, and earlier progress can be archived.

Mission 1: Communication Blackout

The question. Can the player bring the base back online by finding the right satellite and holding a stable radio link?

What the player does.

  • Uses an interactive radar console to find the three satellites overhead and identify the one that matters.
  • Diagnoses and repairs the damaged antenna with materials collected at the base.
  • Turns the dish in small steps until it sits inside a usable alignment window, then holds it there while data packets are acquired.

What the player learns.

  • A radio link needs the antenna pointed at the satellite's bearing, within a tolerance.
  • Signal strength changes as alignment changes, so calibration is a matter of careful adjustment, not guessing.

Mission 2: Shelter Power Emergency

The question. Can the player rebuild the power system and share limited energy so the habitat keeps running?

What the player does.

  • Drags and snaps cables to reconnect the solar panels, the battery and the habitat on a power board.
  • Allocates the available energy between the systems the shelter depends on.
  • Works against the clock, because stored supplies such as food decay while power is down.

What the player learns.

  • A power system is a chain of generation, storage and use, and a break anywhere stops the whole chain.
  • Energy is limited, so allocation is a trade-off between systems.
  • Dust on solar panels reduces power, which links to the NASA solar-array imagery in the Research Terminal.

Mission 3: Rover Rescue

The question. Can the player find a stranded rover in a storm, repair what is needed and drive to it safely?

What the player does.

  • Scans a 3×3 grid of the area and compares Weak, Medium and Strong signals to pick the cell where the rover is. A wrong pick costs a penalty.
  • Repairs the rescue vehicle and plans a route.
  • Drives with heading-based controls through terrain and storm conditions, using the handbrake to stop, and reaches the stranded rover to complete the rescue.

What the player learns.

  • Locating something from signal strength means comparing readings and picking the strongest.
  • Terrain and weather change how a vehicle moves, so route planning matters before driving.

The Research Terminal

The Research Terminal is an optional station that teaches science concepts through a local, offline pack of NASA data. Each item has a catalogue entry with its source, description and status.

Players earn Research Points by completing activities and spend them in the supply store on repair kits and supplies that help in the missions.

Replay and practice

Mission Replay lets a player practice any completed mission without changing campaign unlocks or rewards, which makes the game usable in a classroom where students want to try a mission again.

How the game teaches

Each mission is built around one real Mars-exploration idea and one action the player must take to prove they understand it.

Four design choices keep the learning clear:

  • Feedback in the moment. Meters, penalties, hints after a wrong choice and a mission report show the player what worked and what did not.
  • Pressure that stays fair. Missions are timed so decisions feel real, and a timeout screen handles failure without ending the campaign.
  • Depth on request. Research is optional, so a player who wants only to play can finish, and a player who wants the science can go much further.
  • Practice without risk. Mission Replay lets players try a finished mission again without changing campaign rewards or unlocks.

Accuracy and honesty

The game separates what is real from what is invented.

  • Real and credited. Research images and metadata come from NASA, JPL, the University of Arizona and USGS, and every item is listed in a manifest with its attribution.
  • Never invented. The data pack's rules forbid made-up product IDs or measurements. Where authentic data was not available, such as a numeric MOLA elevation profile, the slot is marked unavailable instead of being filled with invented values.
  • Curated, not raw. The MEDA timeline uses published dust-opacity ranges from a peer-reviewed study, and the game states that it is not a raw data extract.
  • Fictional game values. Habitat power units and mission numbers are game values, not real mission figures.
  • Simplified on purpose. Missions are simplified for learning and do not model real mission operations.

Technology

  • Python 3.10 with Pygame CE for the 2.5D game, with layered parallax backgrounds, procedural art and optional PNG sprites that replace the shapes when present.
  • A shared design system for buttons, panels and mission screens, so every challenge looks and feels consistent.
  • A local, offline NASA research pack made of browse images, per-item metadata JSON and one manifest.
  • Automatic saving to a user folder, with a crash log for troubleshooting.
  • Packaged with PyInstaller as MARSMISSION.exe for Windows, so players need no Python installation.

Who it is for and why it matters

MARSMISSION is aimed at students and curious beginners who have never worked with space data. They get to be mission engineers first and read the science second, so the data feels like a tool and not a lesson.

Because the game runs from a single offline download and saves its own progress, it suits classrooms, clubs and events where internet access is limited or unreliable. Mission Replay lets a teacher or a student repeat a mission as often as they like.

The larger point is that real NASA imagery and published science are already open to everyone, but they are hard to approach. A game is a friendly way in. Players who finish MARSMISSION have used ideas such as signal strength, solar power, dust and terrain to solve problems, and they can follow credited NASA sources to learn more.

Installation guide

MARSMISSION runs on Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit). The packaged build needs no Python or Pygame installation, and the game works offline once installed.

Install on Windows, step by step

  1. Download MARSMISSION_Windows.zip.
  2. Unzip it into a folder you can find again, for example Documents\MARSMISSION. Right-click the zip and choose Extract All, or use any unzip tool.
  3. Open the folder. You should see MARSMISSION.exe, a folder named _internal, and the guide files PLAYER_README.md and SETUP.md.
  4. Keep every file together. MARSMISSION.exe needs the _internal folder next to it, so do not move the .exe on its own.
  5. Double-click MARSMISSION.exe. If Windows Defender blocks the game, allow the folder in Windows Security and launch it again.
  6. The title screen opens. Choose New Campaign to start playing.

Run from source (for developers), step by step

  1. Install Python 3.10 or newer (3.10, 3.11 or 3.12 recommended). Tick Add to PATH during setup.
  2. Open a terminal in the project folder, the one that contains main.py.
  3. Create a virtual environment with python -m venv .venv, then activate it with .venv\Scripts\activate.
  4. Install the requirements with python -m pip install --upgrade pip and then python -m pip install -r requirements.txt. This installs Pygame CE. Do not install pygame and pygame-ce together.
  5. Start the game with python main.py.
  6. Optional check: python -c "import pygame; print(pygame.version.ver)" prints the Pygame version if the install worked.

Where progress is saved

Progress saves automatically to a user folder, outside the game package, so deleting or re-unzipping the game does not erase it.

On Windows, the save folder is %LOCALAPPDATA%\MarsMission\.

Troubleshooting

Game guide: How to play

Controls

Playing the campaign, step by step

  1. On the title screen, choose Continue Campaign to load your save, New Campaign to start fresh (after a confirmation), or Mission Replay to practise a mission you have finished.
  2. Read the mission briefing and press Continue. It explains that a dust storm has damaged the research base.
  3. Explore the base and the outer terrain with the movement keys. Walk up to repair materials and press E to collect them.
  4. Press I to check your inventory and J to read your journal when you need a reminder of what to do next.
  5. Optional: visit the Research Lab at the base and open the Research Terminal. Complete the activities to earn Research Points. Press ESC to leave safely.
  6. Spend Research Points at the supply store on kits that help with repairs.
  7. Walk to a mission station and press E. A short prep screen checks that you are ready. Missions unlock in order, so Challenge 1 comes first.
  8. Play the challenge (see the three walkthroughs below). A timer shows the time left, and a timeout screen appears if it runs out.
  9. Read the debrief and mission report. Finishing a challenge unlocks the next one, and a final report closes the campaign after Challenge 3.
  10. Use Mission Replay to practise any finished mission. Practice runs do not change campaign rewards or unlocks.

Image 1: exploring the base

Image 2: the Research Terminal

Challenge 1: Communication Blackout, step by step

  1. Walk to the communication station and press E to start. The timer appears in the top-right corner.
  2. Diagnose the damaged antenna, then repair it using the materials you collected.
  3. On the radar console, find the three satellites and compare their signals. Choose the one that gives the best link.
  4. On the alignment screen, turn the dish left or right in 5-degree steps until it matches the satellite's bearing and sits inside the usable alignment window.
  5. Hold the dish steady while data packets are acquired. When the link is restored, the completion panel appears. Continue to the debrief.

Image 3: Challenge 1 radar console

Challenge 2: Shelter Power Emergency, step by step

  1. Walk to the power station and press E to start. The timer begins, and stored supplies such as food slowly decay while power is down.
  2. On the wiring screen, drag the cables and let them snap into place to connect the solar panel, the battery and the Mars habitat.
  3. On the power board, allocate the available energy between the shelter's systems.
  4. Confirm the allocation. A message tells you the power circuit is restored. Continue to the debrief.

Image 4: Challenge 2 wiring screen

Challenge 3: Rover Rescue, step by step

  1. Walk to the rescue station and press E to start.
  2. On the scan screen, check the 3×3 grid and read each cell's signal: Weak, Medium or Strong. Pick the cell with the Strong signal. A wrong pick adds a penalty and a hint to look for Strong.
  3. Repair the rescue vehicle with the materials and kits you have.
  4. Plan your route across the terrain before you set off.
  5. Drive with the movement keys. Use Space as a handbrake, and steer clear of obstacles and the worst of the storm.
  6. When you are close to the stranded rover, press E to rescue it. Continue to the debrief and the final report.
